prompt.context: Our client is a ski resort. It is a small slope with little advertising and many surrounding slopes that are far better known. The resort currently outsources concessions, which generates negligible income. The visitor mix is roughly 60% day skiers (single-day visits) and 40% resort skiers (multi-day stays of 3-5 days). The resort serves skiers only — there is no snowboard park or similar amenity. The current day-ski ticket price is $35. Fixed costs are $1,000,000 per year and variable costs are $10 per skier.
prompt.question: The resort currently earns net income of $500,000. The owner wants to increase net income to $1,000,000. Assess the options for achieving this goal.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current ticket price?
Does the resort have any other revenue streams?
clarifying_info.a: Concessions are outsourced and income is negligible

clarifying_info.q: What type of visitors does the resort attract?
clarifying_info.a: 60% day skiers (single day), 40% resort skiers (3-5 day stays)

clarifying_info.q: Does the resort have a snowboard park or other amenities?

clarifying_info.a: There are many surrounding slopes that are far better known

framework: 1. Understand the slope profile: customer mix, revenue sources, cost structure
2. Back into current visitor volume from known financials
3. Calculate visitors needed to hit $1M net income and assess feasibility
4. Brainstorm levers to close the gap (volume, price, mix, cost reduction)
5. Evaluate each idea for revenue uplift, cost impact, cannibalization, and customer fit

questions.prompt: How many skiers does the resort currently serve per year?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use the income statement to back into volume. Net income = Revenue - Fixed costs - Variable costs. Revenue = Price x Volume. With net income $500k, fixed costs $1M, price $35, variable cost $10: $500k = $35Q - $10Q - $1M => $25Q = $1.5M => Q = 60,000 skiers per year.

math.setup: Net Income = (Price - Variable Cost) x Q - Fixed Costs => $500,000 = ($35 - $10) x Q - $1,000,000

questions.prompt: How many skiers per year are needed to reach $1,000,000 in net income, assuming no other changes?
questions.guidance: Same formula with target net income of $1M: $1M = $25Q - $1M => $25Q = $2M => Q = 80,000 skiers. This is a 33% increase in volume — candidate should comment on feasibility given the competitive market and small size of the slope.

math.answer: 80,000 skiers per year — a 33% increase over current 60,000

questions.prompt: What are the ways to reach the $1,000,000 profit target? Evaluate the options.
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure ideas around the three profit levers — volume, price, and cost — and for each idea consider: incremental revenue, incremental cost, cannibalization/trade-offs, and fit with the current customer base. Strong candidates will also note that ideas can be combined. Examples: Night skiing adds volume with modest incremental fixed cost (lighting); snowboard park attracts a new segment but may change resort character; raising prices from $35 increases margin per skier but risks volume loss; increased advertising raises volume but adds cost; new lift expands capacity but requires large capex.

brainstorming.prompt: What specific initiatives could the resort pursue to increase profit to $1,000,000?

categories.name: Volume — attract more skiers
ideas: Night skiing to extend daily operating hours
Increased advertising and marketing spend
Group or corporate packages
Loyalty / season-pass programs
Partnerships with nearby hotels or travel agencies

categories.name: Product Mix / New Segments
ideas: Add a snowboard park to attract snowboarders
Terrain variety (beginner, intermediate, expert trails)
Ski school or lessons for beginners
Tubing or non-ski winter activities
Summer activities (mountain biking, hiking) for year-round revenue

categories.name: Price
ideas: Raise day-ticket price above $35 (test price elasticity)
Dynamic pricing (peak weekend vs. weekday rates)
Premium lift-line passes
Package pricing for resort skiers (lift + lodging bundles)

categories.name: Cost Reduction
ideas: Renegotiate supplier contracts
Energy efficiency investments (snowmaking, lighting)
Staffing optimization in off-peak periods

categories.name: Revenue per Visitor
ideas: In-source concessions to capture food and beverage margin
Ski rental or equipment sales
Retail merchandise

categories.name: Strategic
ideas: Partner with or co-market alongside well-known neighboring slopes
Seek a niche positioning (e.g., family-friendly, uncrowded, value)
Targeted advertising to 40% resort-skier segment for higher per-visit spend

recommendation: The resort needs to grow from 60,000 to 80,000 skiers, or find an equivalent profit improvement through price increases or new revenue streams

A combination of moderate price increase (e.g., $35 to $40, adding $5 x 60,000 = $300,000 incremental margin) and a targeted volume initiative such as night skiing or a snowboard park is the most balanced path
This hybrid approach reduces reliance on any single lever and is achievable without a dramatic change to the resort's character
risks: Price increase may reduce volume if the market is price-sensitive, especially against better-known competing slopes
Adding a snowboard park or new lift requires significant upfront capex that may delay or offset profit gains
Increased advertising spend adds fixed cost, raising the breakeven visitor count
next_steps: Conduct price sensitivity research among current day-skier segment
Model capex and payback period for night skiing infrastructure
Survey customers on interest in snowboard park or other amenities
Evaluate co-marketing opportunities with neighboring slopes to share advertising cost
